title: Fire and the blade of grass
hookLine: the gods say a victory is theirs, and fire can't burn one blade of grass: asmita, the seer mistaken for its instruments
carry: asmita: the seer mistaken for what it sees
tomorrow: a king gives up a whole kingdom. can a baby deer undo him?
last: AVIDYA: TAKING WHAT PASSES FOR WHAT LASTS.

cards: The Kena Upanishad tells a story about a victory. The gods have beaten the demons, and they celebrate: this win is ours, this greatness is ours. But the power behind it was Brahman's, the one reality in everything.
So Brahman appears as a strange, wonderful being the gods can't place. They send Agni, god of fire, to find out. Who are you? it asks.
I'm Agni, he says. I can burn anything on earth. It sets down one blade of grass.

teach.h: AGNI CAN'T BURN ONE BLADE OF GRASS.
teach.b: Agni rushes at it with all his speed, and the grass doesn't even singe. Then Vayu, the wind: I can carry off anything on earth. He can't stir the blade.
Then Indra, king of the gods, goes himself, and the being vanishes. In its place stands a radiant woman, Uma, daughter of the mountains. She tells him: that was Brahman.
The victory was Brahman's, and you were taking it as yours. The Upanishad's opening names what's underneath: the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the eye of the eye.
Not what you see; what you see by. Now Patanjali, sutra 2.6. Asmita, I-ness, from asmi, I am, is when the seer and the power of seeing seem to be one self.
Drig, the seer. Darshana shakti, the power of seeing, here the mind. And one small, crucial word: iva, as if.
They only seem to be one. That's Agni's mistake in a single line: the fire took the power moving through it as its own. Asmita isn't arrogance; a shy person has as much as a loud one.
It's the glue that sticks awareness to the body, the moods, the story of me.

teach.h: 2.6: SEER AND INSTRUMENT, AS IF ONE.
teach.b: The Upanishads call the seer the atman, and this is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: you are the one who sees, not the instrument.
It's one reason many Hindu families, after a win, say first: by God's grace.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO SEES, NOT THE INSTRUMENT.
teach.b: Today it's the grade, the goal, the post that soars or flops, and it feels like the whole of who you are. Remember the blade of grass. Notice the one who's looking.

how: The Kena Upanishad's story of the gods and the blade of grass is a well-loved teaching about where power really comes from. In classical yoga, asmita is loosened through discernment between the seer and the seen; teachers often have students notice the difference between awareness and the thoughts and roles it is aware of, and many Hindus credit a success to God's grace before their own effort.

o: a proud, boastful sense of being better
a healthy confidence in your own worth
asmita: seer and mind seeming to be one self

games.q: the blade of grass and the sutra — tap the pairs.
p: can't burn one blade of grass
as if: they only seem one

s: Agni burned the blade of grass in one breath
he rushed at it with all his speed and it didn't even singe. the power he called his own wasn't his alone.
asmita is just another word for arrogance
a shy person has as much as a loud one. it's the glue that sticks awareness to the mind.
the word iva in 2.6 means 'as if'
the seer and the mind only seem to be one.

games.q: Agni boasts he can burn anything on earth, then can't burn one blade of grass. by sutra 2.6, what was his mistake?
o: he took the power moving through him as his own 'I': seer and instrument, as if one.
he just needed more practice at burning.
games.why: ekatmata iva: as if one. the fire took the power moving through it as 'mine'; Uma tells Indra it was Brahman's all along.

practice: Say silently, I am, and notice what comes with it: a feeling in the chest, a picture of your face, a name, a role. Then notice that you are aware of all of it, and gently ask whether the one who sees is one more thing on the list.
You don't need an answer; let the question loosen the glue a little.

wordCard.voice: I-ness. Asmita, sutra 2.6: the seer and the mind it sees through seem to be one self. Seem, as if, iva, is the key.

orig.note: Sanskrit asmitā: I-ness, from asmi, 'I am'. the second of the five afflictions.

carryVoice: Your line: asmita, the seer mistaken for what it sees. Remember the blade of grass. See you tomorrow.
